competencies.definition: Conveying ideas clearly to others in speech and writing; does not count a single named channel such as presentations or documentation, which have their own entries.
Writing that is clear and well structured for its reader (memos, specs, updates); does not count spoken communication or software documentation tooling.
Speaking clearly and persuasively in conversation and meetings; does not count written work or formal presentations.
Preparing and delivering presentations to an audience; does not count day-to-day conversation or writing.
Communicating and reporting to senior leadership and executives; does not count general stakeholder communication with peers.
Shaping facts and strategy into a compelling narrative for an audience; does not count plain reporting.
Building relationships with, and managing the expectations of, the people a product affects; does not count aligning peers by influence alone or customer research.
Moving people and decisions without formal authority over them; does not count managing a reporting line.
aliases: ability to influence technical and business stakeholders

competencies.definition: Working well with colleagues in general; does not count collaboration specifically across functions, which is cross-functional-collaboration.
Getting along and working well with other people one on one and in groups; does not count formal communication channels such as communication or presentation, nor influencing without authority.
Working productively with other functions such as engineering, design, sales and operations; does not count leading those teams.
Leading initiatives that span several functions or teams without owning them; does not count line management or ordinary collaboration.
Reaching agreements on terms, scope or priorities with another party; does not count general influence.
Running workshops and meetings so a group reaches a decision; does not count presenting.
Breaking a problem into parts and reasoning about it with evidence; does not count operating a specific analytics tool or method.
Finding practical solutions to unclear or difficult problems; does not count purely analytical reporting.
Questioning assumptions and weighing evidence before deciding; does not count problem solving in general.
Setting long-term direction and trading off options against goals; does not count planning a single project.
Ranking competing work by value, cost and urgency and saying no; does not count maintaining a backlog as such.
Making sound decisions with incomplete information; does not count using data as the basis, which is data-driven decision making.
Basing product and business decisions on data and measured results; does not count the technical work of analysing data.
Understanding how a business makes money and what drives its results; does not count product judgment or pricing expertise.
Judgment about what makes a product valuable and usable to its users; does not count general business judgment.
Understanding technology well enough to discuss tradeoffs with engineers; does not count hands-on engineering in a named stack.
A past career or education in engineering or another technical field; does not count technical fluency gained only on the job as a product person.
Understanding and caring about the situation and feelings of users; does not count running user research.
Putting customer needs first in decisions; does not count customer research methods.
Noticing and correcting small errors in one's own and others' work; does not count formal quality assurance.
Keeping work, information and commitments in order; does not count time management as such.
Planning one's own time to meet deadlines; does not count prioritizing a team's work.
Taking responsibility for an outcome from start to finish; does not count initiative alone.
Acting without being asked and moving things forward; does not count working alone.
Working without close supervision; does not count taking initiative to start new work.
A habit of asking questions and learning new things; does not count a stated interest in one subject.
Acting like an owner of the business, comfortable with risk and building something new; does not count having founded a company.
Making progress where goals or information are unclear; does not count flexibility about priorities.
Working in a setting with quick change and short deadlines; does not count startup experience.
Honesty and consistent ethical conduct; does not count compliance knowledge.
Defining where a product is going and why, and how it wins; does not count planning the next releases, which is roadmapping.
aliases: define and communicate product vision and strategy

competencies.definition: Building and maintaining a product roadmap that sequences work over time; does not count setting the strategy it serves.
aliases: experience owning or driving roadmap strategy and definition

competencies.definition: Finding out which problems are worth solving before building, by research, testing and prototypes; does not count delivering what was already decided.
aliases: solid understanding of product discovery practices

competencies.definition: Learning customer problems and needs by direct contact with customers; does not count analysing usage data.
Studying user behaviour and needs with interviews, surveys and observation; does not count analysing product metrics.
Interviewing customers or users to understand their problems; does not count surveys or analytics.
Studying a market's size, segments and trends; does not count analysing specific competitors.
Analysing competitors' products and positioning; does not count general market sizing.
Building the financial and strategic case for an investment; does not count day-to-day budgeting.
Writing product requirements, specs or PRDs that engineers can build from; does not count eliciting needs or user stories alone.
Writing user stories with their context and intent; does not count full specifications.
Defining testable acceptance criteria for a piece of work; does not count writing the stories themselves.
Keeping a product backlog groomed, ordered and ready for the team; does not count the strategy or roadmap above it.
Designing and running experiments, including A/B tests, to test product hypotheses; does not count analysing usage metrics without an experiment.
Measuring how a product is used with analytics tools and metrics; does not count running experiments or general data analysis.
Analysing conversion funnels to find drop-off; does not count general product analytics.
Defining success metrics, KPIs and OKRs and tracking them; does not count analysing the underlying data.
Planning how a product reaches its market: positioning, channels, launch plan; does not count the engineering delivery of the launch.
Taking a product or feature from ready to released to customers; does not count the go-to-market strategy behind it.
Setting prices, packaging and ways of earning revenue from a product; does not count general financial planning.
Having taken a product through its whole lifecycle from idea to launch and improvement; does not count owning one stage only.
Shipping product features with attention to scope and tradeoffs; does not count owning the whole product lifecycle.
aliases: experience with product feature delivery and tradeoffs
experience with feature delivery and product tradeoffs

competencies.definition: Building quick prototypes or mockups to test ideas; does not count production design or engineering.
Planning and coordinating the release of software to production; does not count product launch marketing.
Planning and driving a project to its deadline, scope and budget; does not count program management across projects or product management.
Coordinating several related projects toward one goal; does not count managing a single project.
Guiding people and organizations through a change in tools or ways of working; does not count release management.
Identifying, assessing and mitigating risks to a plan or business; does not count regulatory compliance as such.
Redesigning how work is done to make it faster or better; does not count automating a single task.
Analysing business needs and processes and turning them into requirements; does not count writing the product specification itself.
Writing and maintaining documentation for processes, products or systems; does not count specs written to drive a build, which is requirements writing.
Setting direction and motivating others toward it; does not count line management or technical leadership as such.
Managing a team of direct reports: hiring, feedback, performance; does not count leading without reports.
Coaching less experienced colleagues; does not count managing them.
Having mentored or coached other product managers; does not count mentoring in other functions.
Guiding the technical direction of a team or product; does not count people management.
Understanding what APIs are and how products use them; does not count designing APIs or writing integrations, and the REST and GraphQL terms are in the skills dictionary.
Designing the contract and shape of an API; does not count merely using one.
Knowing software development kits and how developers consume them; does not count building one in a specific language.
Knowing the stages of building and releasing software; does not count a particular methodology, which Agile and Scrum cover.
Knowing how software is tested and quality assured; does not count unit testing frameworks, which are in the skills dictionary.
Knowing how development and operations teams build, release and run software together; does not count a specific CI/CD tool.
Automating repetitive work with scripts or tools; does not count building automation platforms.
Monitoring and understanding the running state of systems with logs, metrics and traces; does not count business analytics.
Understanding systems spread across several machines and their tradeoffs; does not count single-server application design.
General understanding of cloud infrastructure and services; does not count a named provider, which is in the skills dictionary.
Knowing how data is moved and transformed between systems; does not count analysing the result.
Designing the structure of data and its relationships; does not count writing queries.
Policies and controls for data ownership, access and quality; does not count privacy regulation alone.
aliases: practical understanding of data governance principles

competencies.definition: Keeping data accurate, complete and consistent; does not count governance policy.
General understanding of information and application security; does not count identity management or compliance frameworks.
Products and concepts for identity, login and access control; does not count general security.
Rules and practice for protecting personal data; does not count general security or data governance.
Meeting legal and regulatory requirements in a sector; does not count risk management in general.
Large language models and generative AI as a product capability; does not count classical machine learning, which is in the skills dictionary.
AI agents and agentic workflows built on language models; does not count generative AI features that are not agentic.
Grounding language-model answers in retrieved documents; does not count fine-tuning.
Writing prompts and instructions that steer a language model; does not count evaluating its output.
Safe, fair and accountable use of AI, including guardrails; does not count general compliance.
Having been a product manager for technical products or working closely with engineering as a technical PM; does not count a non-technical product role.
aliases: experience working as a technical product manager
experience managing technical products or online services

competencies.definition: Managing platform or infrastructure products used by other teams or developers; does not count an end-user application.
Products built for developers: tools, platforms and developer experience; does not count a product that merely has an API.
Platforms with third-party developers or partners building on them; does not count a closed product.
Subscription software delivered over the web; does not count on-premise software.
Products sold to businesses rather than consumers; does not count consumer products.
Two-sided marketplaces that connect buyers and sellers; does not count a single-seller shop.
Having worked at an early-stage or fast-growing company; does not count a large corporation's innovation team.
Financial technology products and companies; does not count banking operations as such.
Payment products and processing; does not count lending or trading.
Retail, corporate or digital banking; does not count other financial services.
The financial-services industry in general; does not count the narrower sectors of banking, payments and trading.
Trading, brokerage and investment products; does not count payments or banking.
Online selling of goods and services; does not count physical retail alone.
The retail industry; does not count online-only commerce, which is ecommerce.
Transport, delivery and supply-chain operations; does not count warehouse software alone.
Technology for healthcare providers and patients; does not count general wellness apps.
Software for human resources, payroll and workforce management; does not count internal HR work.
Advertising technology and programmatic advertising; does not count marketing work in general.
The video game industry; does not count a personal interest in games.
A completed bachelor's-level university degree in any field; does not count a master's degree or a stated field of study.
aliases: bachelor's degree or equivalent practical experience
bachelor's degree in a relevant field

competencies.definition: A completed master's-level degree; does not count an MBA or a bachelor's degree.
A graduate degree, either a master's or a doctorate, unspecified; does not count an MBA named alone or a bachelor's degree.
A Master of Business Administration; does not count other master's degrees.
